title: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, a memo shows
authors: Ryan J. Foley, “Lethal Restraint.” twitter mailto, apnews.com, ryan-j-foley
description:
The new guidance comes after ICE-initiated vehicle stops have repeatedly escalated when drivers have refused to cooperate or tried to flee.
After fatal shootings of drivers in Maine and Texas in July, ICE officers were directed to temporarily pause most vehicle stops.
“Vehicle stops and arrests of illegal aliens continue.” The new memo outlines steps intended to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE officers, drivers they are targeting, their passengers and the public.
All officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras, under the guidance.
In addition, only officers who have completed one of five specific agency training courses can conduct vehicle stops.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have been ordered not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training, under new internal guidance issued after several drivers were shot in encounters with ICE.

A memo sent to officers in ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division and obtained by The Associated Press warned they are not authorized to chase vehicles that fail to pull over under any circumstances. Instead, officers should take down the vehicles’ information for further investigation, according to the memo signed by ICE’s executive associate director Marcos D. Charles and dated Wednesday.

The new guidance comes after ICE-initiated vehicle stops have repeatedly escalated when drivers have refused to cooperate or tried to flee. ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen such encounters since last year, killing at least four people and wounding several others.

President Donald Trump’s administration has faced internal tension over how to handle traffic stops, which are seen as particularly high-risk encounters.

After fatal shootings of drivers in Maine and Texas in July, ICE officers were directed to temporarily pause most vehicle stops. But the next day, Trump went on social media to direct the agency to continue traffic stops, calling them “one of ICE’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools.”

ICE has faced intense pressure from the White House to deport more people who are in the country illegally, and its arrests have reached record numbers. At the same time, the agency’s rapid hiring spree last year resulted in some poorly vetted and trained officers hitting the streets.

In a statement, ICE downplayed the significance of the memo, which said the new guidance was intended to replace and amend prior directives issued earlier this year, last year and in 2018.

“Occasionally, ICE leadership issues guidance reminders to law enforcement officers,” the statement said. “Vehicle stops and arrests of illegal aliens continue.”

The new memo outlines steps intended to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE officers, drivers they are targeting, their passengers and the public.

The memo told ICE’s field office directors that they must ensure vehicles used for traffic stops have lights and sirens that let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles when activated. All officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras, under the guidance.

In addition, only officers who have completed one of five specific agency training courses can conduct vehicle stops. Officers who have not completed the training courses can only participate in vehicle stops “in a support capacity” as passengers and cannot be the drivers of any of the vehicles involved.

The guidance says ICE officers can continue to use a controversial technique known as pinning, which is defined as “using a vehicle or physical barrier to trap or stop a car,” but only if they have received special training. Similarly, only trained officers can use spike strips that deflate tires to prevent drivers from fleeing.

The memo came the day that courtroom testimony highlighted ways in which two ICE officers involved in a vehicle stop, pursuit and shooting that wounded a delivery driver in Austin last month would not have complied with the new guidance.

During a bond hearing for Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, testimony showed that the officer who shot him wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The ICE officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned it off during the pursuit.

Prosecutors presented surveillance video that showed an ICE agent chasing Garces Perez at high speeds through residential streets after he fled an initial traffic stop.

Garces Perez faces federal assault charges after investigators say he struck an ICE officer with his driver’s side mirror. That officer then shot into Perez’s vehicle, lodging a bullet in his back, officials say.

Attorneys for Garces Perez have called the charges against him “retaliation” and have argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn’t fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee.

___

Associated Press reporter Anna Wilder contributed to this report from Austin, Texas.

text:
FAIR shows administration’s policies are unreviewable

WASHINGTON—Today, the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) filed a brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit urging the court to vacate an injunction issued by the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island against tough vetting procedures and exclusions the Trump Administration has put in place for aliens, especially those from countries that do not keep reliable records. The plaintiffs challenge the policies under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), claiming they are contrary to law and “arbitrary and capricious.”

FAIR, while not conceding that these claims have any merit, shows in its brief that the vetting and exclusion policies, issued by the Department of Homeland Security, were made to carry out an executive order the President gave pursuant to his inherent foreign-affairs powers and a number of Proclamations he made under a statute that empowers him to suspend the entry of any aliens in the national interest. The President is not an agency, and so his actions cannot be reviewed by courts under the APA. And actions by his subordinates to carry out his orders given under foreign-affairs or statutory presidential authority are presidential actions, too, and equally unreviewable.

“Finally we have a President whose concern about national security is very real,” said Dale L. Wilcox, executive director and general counsel of FAIR. “But when he acts squarely within his broad powers to keep us safe from future and potential threats, an activist court pretends his actions can be reviewed under the run-of-the-mill standard governing agencies when they exercise regulatory power Congress delegated to them. But no law gives courts the authority to second-guess how the President exercises either his inherent foreign-policy powers or his discretion given to him by law. The court should recognize the magnitude of the constitutional error that was committed by the lower court and throw this case out for lack of jurisdiction.”

The case is Dorcas International Institute of Rhode Island v. United States Citizen and Immigration Services, No. 26-1703 (First Circuit).

text:
RICHLAND — Candidates for Washington’s most conservative congressional district clashed Wednesday night over rising costs, a federal immigration crackdown and the reach of presidential power.

Amanda McKinney, a Republican and former banker, is now a Yakima County commissioner endorsed by President Donald Trump.

John Duresky, a Democrat, is a U.S. Air Force veteran who later worked at the Hanford Field Office until last year, when he took an early retirement offer during the president’s DOGE cuts.

The open seat in Washington’s 4th Congressional District comes after six-term U.S. Rep Dan Newhouse, R-Sunnyside, announced his retirement in late December. Newhouse was one of the last Republicans in Congress who voted to impeach Trump after a mob of his supporters breached the Capitol building on Jan. 6, 2021.

In the August top-two primary, in a field of 11 candidates, McKinney pulled 35% and Duresky 30%, with Republicans Jerrod Sessler and Matt Boenhke getting 15% and 11%, respectively. Duresky is now hoping to ride a midterm blue wave to a major upset, in a solid red district where the last general election featured two Republicans.

Affordability

From the first question of the debate, the candidates sparred over rising gasoline and grocery costs, as well as record diesel prices.

Duresky blamed the nation’s attack on Iran and tariffs implemented by Trump in his second administration. Duresky said any tariffs should be set by Congress, not the president.

Meanwhile, “the war in Iran has led to higher fuel prices, inputs to fertilizer, inflation,” he said.

McKinney laid the blame on laws passed by Washington state’s Democratic establishment, such as the recent ban on more natural gas and mandates for clean energy, like wind and solar power.

“It’s false to say the tariffs and the war in Iran are responsible for high prices,” she said.

The debate, put together by AARP Washington, local League of Women Voters chapters and Northwest Public Broadcasting, was held at Washington State University’s Tri-Cities campus. The forum had no audience but was streamed and is available to watch on NWPB’s YouTube channel.

Immigration

On immigration, both candidates broadly supported expanding the federal H-2A guest worker program to help bring workers into Central Washington’s orchards and other agricultural businesses.

Advertising

“But they must go home, because we want people in our country legally,” McKinney said.

She also expressed support for the Trump administration’s push to deport immigrants — which has not spared Central Washington — and criticized the sanctuary laws passed in the state Legislature, which in some cases prevent local law enforcement from talking to federal agents.

“Grateful for the Trump administration for highlighting Washington state sanctuary policies are putting law enforcement officers at risk,” she said.

Duresky slammed the president’s deportation program, calling it “immoral and un-American.”

“This country was built on immigration, and right here in Central Washington we have built so much prosperity from immigrants,” Duresky said, adding that he does not believe in open borders.

‘Kitchen table issues’

McKinney has described her campaign as focusing on “kitchen table issues,” such as driving down energy costs and investing in nuclear power and other energy production. She also has said officials need to do more to solve Central Washington’s water issues, which the district’s farms and agricultural industry depend upon.

Duresky called for restoring the Affordable Care Act healthcare subsidies, strengthening labor protections and raising the federal minimum wage.

During the debate, host Matt Loveless, an assistant professor at WSU’s Edward R. Murrow College of Communication, read a question submitted by a citizen about congressional powers over spending, war and other areas.

“It seems like Congress has given up their role,” the question began. “So if elected, would you be compelling to balance and check the executive branch … or are you satisfied with the amount of power the executive branch has in the current system?”

McKinney said “voters are absolutely correct in always wanting to see the tensions” between the president, Congress and the U.S. Supreme Court.

She suggested that members of Congress have more information than voters, on issues like the Iran war.

“Inaction by Congress right now is not to me a judgment that they are inept,” she said. “It simply means that the information that they’ve been presented continues to convince them that they should continue to support the president’s actions thus far.”

Duresky cited a pledge that he’s taken called the “Take BAC Congress pledge” that some Democratic candidates have signed.

“It Includes term limits, a ban on stock trading by sitting congressmen, a moratorium on lobbying by departing congressmen, overturning (the Supreme Court decision) Citizens United to get unlimited money out of politics, and finally, an enforceable ethics code for the Supreme Court,” he said. “We think that helps fix Congress.”

Asked which congressional committees they would like to be appointed to if they win, McKinney said she wanted to work on appropriations, which directs federal spending; Duresky said he wanted to work on agriculture issues.

Washington’s 4th Congressional District runs down the middle of Washington from its northern to southern border, and includes all of Douglas, Okanogan, Benton, Grant, Yakima and Klickitat counties, and small parts of Adams and Franklin counties.

Ballots for the November general election are set to be mailed out by Oct. 16.

text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), and Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) led six of their colleagues in demanding the Trump Administration abandon a plan that would prevent up to 700,000 Deferred Action on Childhood Arrivals (DACA) and Temporary Protected Status (TPS) recipients and other tax-paying immigrants from claiming tax credits they are eligible for.

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the Department of Treasury are proposing a rule change that would prevent hundreds of thousands of taxpayers from claiming the Adoption Tax Credit, the American Opportunity Tax Credit, the Child Tax Credit, and the Earned Income Tax Credit. DACA and TPS recipients have been lawfully claiming these taxes for decades.

“According to your own estimates, the proposed rule change could affect up to 700,000 taxpayers,” the Senators wrote in a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and IRS CEO Frank Bisignano. “This would include more than 300,000 individuals living in households with a DACA recipient, two-thirds of whom are U.S. citizens and who have, on average, lived in the United States for over 28 years. The practical effect of these new regulations would be to deny tax credits to immigrants who are legally eligible for them and lawfully present in our country, and to create a byzantine and unworkable system for both tax preparers and taxpayers.”

“The Administration has no legal authority to change congressionally enacted tax law via regulation…” they continued. “Since the passage of PRWORA in 1996, no federal agency has interpreted refundable tax credits as federal public benefits restricted to qualified immigrants. If Congress intended for refundable tax credits to be treated as federal public benefits, it has had over 30 years to clarify the statute.”

“The proposed rule is clear regulatory overreach that would have disastrous impacts for lawfully present immigrants and their families who are legally eligible for refundable tax credits,” they concluded.

In addition to Senators Cortez Masto, Wyden, and Durbin, the letter was signed by Senators Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), and Patty Murray (D-Wash.). The full text of the letter is available here.

The first and only Latina Senator, Cortez Masto has consistently supported immigrant communities in Nevada. She has called on both the Biden and Trump Administrations to protect Dreamers, TPS holders, and other immigrants. Cortez Masto has worked to pass meaningful immigration reform that balances critical border security measures with a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers. Earlier this year, the Senator attended and spoke at a naturalization ceremony for new American citizens at the Sand Harbor Amphitheater at Lake Tahoe, Nevada.

text:
The family of Renee Nicole Good — the 37-year-old mother of three who was fatally shot by an immigration officer in Minneapolis earlier this year — filed a sweeping civil rights lawsuit accusing senior Trump administration officials of orchestrating a discriminatory immigration operation that ultimately led to her killing.

The 149-page complaint, filed nearly nine months after Good was shot inside her SUV, names Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Jonathan Ross along with some of the officials who oversaw the administration’s immigration enforcement campaign: White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, border czar Tom Homan, Corey Lewandowski, then-acting ICE director Todd Lyons, former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino and 10 unidentified federal agents. Each is being sued individually.

"Our country cannot tolerate unjustified and excessive use of force, let alone deadly force, on ordinary people who are exercising their rights under the Constitution of this country," Antonio M. Romanucci, an attorney representing Good’s relatives, said during an Oct. 1 news conference. "There is no such thing as impunity when it comes to violating protected rights. When government power crosses the line, there must be accountability."

At the heart of the lawsuit is an unusual civil rights claim invoking the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871. Good’s family alleges the officials conspired to use Operation Metro Surge to deprive Minnesota’s Somali and Hispanic communities of equal protection under the law — and to intimidate, arrest or use force against people who observed, documented or warned others about the operation.

The complaint argues that Good’s killing on Jan. 7 was a product of that campaign. She and her partner had encountered federal agents in their south Minneapolis neighborhood after dropping her 6-year-old son off at school, according to the lawsuit. Her partner, Becca Good, got out of their SUV to film while Good remained behind the wheel and honked her horn to warn neighbors that immigration officers were nearby.

“Renee was killed in the course of conduct that served both of those objects,” the complaint alleges, arguing she was targeted while “engaged in observing and warning” about the federal operation.

The lawsuit separately accuses Ross of violating Good's Fourth Amendment rights by using excessive force in fatally shooting her. It alleges Good was unarmed, suspected of no crime and slowly turning her SUV away from Ross when he fired three times — once through the windshield and twice through the open driver’s-side window. The complaint says Ross had already moved his body out of the vehicle’s path before opening fire.

The family also alleges the shooting violated mandatory Department of Homeland Security policies restricting officers from firing at the driver of a moving vehicle and from intentionally putting themselves in a vehicle’s path. After Good was shot and her SUV crashed into a parked vehicle, the complaint says, federal agents did not render medical aid and turned away a bystander who identified himself as a physician.

In a separate lawsuit, the family sued the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act, alleging wrongful death and assault, battery, false imprisonment and negligence. The complaint also seeks damages for the emotional harm Becca Good says she suffered from witnessing her partner’s killing.

"Every morning, she is my first thought," Becca Good said in her first public remarks. "I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama and how I will grow old without the love of my life. I think about how we should have had 40 more years together. But I also think about what she would have wanted after all of this."

"What happened to us should never happen to any family," she added.

DHS did not respond to USA TODAY's requests for comment. In a statement, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the Trump administration intends to "vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits."

The suits open a new front in the long-running fight over Good’s death, which was captured from several angles on video and quickly became the subject of sharply conflicting accounts from the federal government, local officials and Good’s family.

Good, a U.S. citizen, was not the target of the immigration operation underway that Jan. 7 morning

Federal agents were deployed across the Minneapolis area as part of Operation Metro Surge, a massive immigration enforcement operation that brought roughly 2,000 additional officers to Minnesota and followed similar enforcement surges in other Democratic-led cities under Noem.

The operation had already drawn fierce opposition from state and local officials, who accused the Trump administration of singling out Minnesota and other Democratic jurisdictions for aggressive federal enforcement. The administration said the deployments were necessary to enforce immigration law in places where local officials would not cooperate with federal authorities.

Good and her partner had stopped near federal agents working in their south Minneapolis neighborhood when they approached her SUV. Video shows officers ordering Good out of the vehicle before she reversed and then began driving forward. Ross, who was standing near the front driver’s side of the SUV, fired three shots.

Noem said Ross fired "defensive shots," arguing Good had tried to use her vehicle as a weapon against him. She said Good was engaged in an act of "domestic terrorism."

In response to the lawsuits, the White House pointed to President Donald Trump’s previous comments about Good. While continuing to defend the immigration operation, Trump said he believed Good "under normal circumstances, was a very solid, wonderful person — but her actions were pretty tough."

"When you look at the way that car was pulled away… there are a couple versions of that tape that are very, very bad," Trump said.

But the circumstances surrounding the shooting were disputed almost immediately. Videos from the scene showed Good turning the steering wheel as she accelerated and did not clearly establish whether the Good's SUV struck Ross.

The killing, as well as the subsequent fatal shooting of 37-year-old Alex Pretti by Customs and Border Protection agents Raymundo Gutierrez and Jesus Ochoa, sparked widespread protests and became a flashpoint in the Trump administration's push for mass deportations.

An independent autopsy commissioned by Good’s family later found three gunshot paths: one through her left forearm, another through the right side of her chest and a third that entered near her left temple and exited the other side of her head. The Hennepin County Medical Examiner classified her death as a homicide, a designation indicating she died at the hands of another person but not, by itself, a determination that a crime occurred.

Hennepin County prosecutors, the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension and the state attorney general’s office continued investigating and eventually sued the federal government for access to evidence, including Good’s SUV, videos, witness interviews and records related to the officers involved.

After months of resistance, federal authorities turned over hard drives containing previously withheld evidence in July, along with Good’s bullet-damaged SUV. State investigators said at the time that they had begun reviewing the material and had not prejudged whether criminal charges were warranted.

Good’s family retained Chicago-based firm Romanucci & Blandin days after her death. The law firm, which also represented George Floyd’s family, launched its own civil investigation and sent the federal government a letter seeking records, video, communications and physical evidence related to the shooting.

Her brother, Brent Ganger, brought the lawsuit as trustee for her next of kin, including her three children, parents and siblings. Becca Good is also a plaintiff in her own right. She was standing feet from the SUV when Ross fired and ran after the vehicle after the shooting, finding her partner with a gunshot wound to the head, according to the complaint. The lawsuit says she has since been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and insomnia.

The family is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, with the amount to be determined at trial.

Suing federal law enforcement officers presents legal obstacles that generally do not exist in cases against local police. Claims against the federal government can proceed under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which waives federal immunity for certain wrongdoing by government employees but imposes procedural limits and does not allow punitive damages or jury trials. Lawsuits seeking damages directly from federal officers for alleged constitutional violations have also been sharply restricted by a series of Supreme Court decisions.

In the months since her death, Good’s family has tried to make sure she is remembered for more than the circumstances of her killing. Her brothers, Luke and Brent Ganger, testified before Congress in February, describing their sister as a devoted mother who was “unapologetically hopeful.”

“Her children were and are her heart walking around outside her body,” Brent Ganger said, reading from the eulogy he delivered at her funeral. “And she made sure they felt safe, valued, and endlessly loved.”

Her parents later described a daughter who loved sparkles, laughter and celebrations and had recently begun working as a substitute teacher.

text:
He’s a Kansas Army National Guardsman and feels betrayed by the country he enlisted to serve just two years ago. His father, an undocumented immigrant from Mexico, sits inside a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in Leavenworth without bail after being arrested in Anderson County, Kansas, for driving with an expired license.

Louis Martinez, 23, of Kansas City, Kansas, was born and raised in Wyandotte County. His parents came to the United States 25 years ago in search of a better life, Martinez told me recently. He said he’s had conflicting feelings about his military commitment since federal immigration authorities placed a detainer on his father, William Israel Martinez Ruiz, also of KCK.

“I know these are tough times,” Martinez said. “But if someone is in the process of becoming a legal citizen, and he’s not a criminal or anything and has been working here for almost all their life and all he does is just be a family man and take care of his family and just work, work, work, it seems really unfair that he’s being treated like a criminal.”

Ruiz has a bond hearing Oct. 14, Martinez said. Under President Donald Trump’s heavy-handed approach to immigration enforcement, even non-violent undocumented Kansans like Ruiz are being arrested, detained and deported. Martinez said he fears the worst for his father despite a pending application to legally remain in the country.

Michael Sharma-Crawford, Ruiz’s immigration attorney, declined to comment for this column.

“The only crime he committed was a traffic violation. It should have just been a fine,” Martinez said.

ICE officials have held Ruiz, a longtime construction worker, at the Midwest Regional Reception Center since Aug. 26.

“Anderson County Sheriff’s Office arrested William Israel Martinez Ruiz, 42, an illegal alien from Mexico, Aug. 24 in Garnett, Kansas, for operating a motor vehicle without a valid license,” ICE officials wrote in an email sent to me. “ICE placed a detainer on Ruiz Aug. 24 and arrested him Aug. 26 for being unlawfully present in the United States.”

In its statement, ICE contends that Ruiz had another minor run-in with the law in 2024 that did little to convince that he was a violent criminal that needed to be deported.

According to immigration officials, the U.S. Army arrested Ruiz Feb. 9, 2024, in Quantico, Virginia, for federal trespassing after he unlawfully entered a military base — an arrest Martinez immediately disputed. When I asked Martinez about the alleged Virginia incident during our interview, he expressed genuine confusion.

“He’s never been to Virginia,” Martinez said.

As it turns out, ICE’s paperwork got the location wrong: Martinez later clarified that his father’s trespassing arrest on Feb. 9, 2024, actually occurred at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri. Court records Martinez forwarded to me from the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri show that prosecutors dismissed the case.

In a follow-up email, I asked ICE officials to clarify the conflicting information, but I hadn’t received any updates as of Tuesday.

“Ruiz remains in ICE custody pending removal and will receive due process under federal law,” immigration officials wrote in their initial email.

Anderson County arrest

According to Martinez, on the day of his father’s arrest, his parents and wife had just dropped him off at a National Guard Armory facility in Coffeyville, a small, historic city in southeast Kansas near the Oklahoma border.

That night, an Anderson County Sheriff’s Deputy pulled over Ruiz on his way home from dropping off Martinez and saw that his license was expired, Martinez told me. The deputy started questioning everyone in the car about their legal status in the country, according to Martinez.

“Afterwards, he was asked to step out and was interrogated by (the deputy),” Martinez wrote in a letter to The Star, which prompted this column. “My dad gave everything showing he was in process for the Military Parole in Place (program) and even gave the immigration lawyer’s information.”

In the letter, Martinez said deputies arrested his father without reading his Miranda rights to him.

“They said he was illegal and didn’t have the right to a lawyer or see a judge,” Martinez wrote. “He was held for 48 hours (until) ICE grabbed him and took him to Leavenworth. I feel betrayed that my country treats its service members’ families like this while on a mission.”

When we spoke for this column, Martinez emphasized the emotional toll the arrest has taken. He had just been activated for a disaster relief mission after significant storms tore through Wyandotte County, which included his hometown of KCK, on Aug. 19.

“I love my country, I love my state,” Martinez said. “It just feels wrong knowing that you’re still serving, and they’re treating your father like this. It’s been a heavy toll on me and especially my family.”

Parole program for noncitizens

According to Martinez, after he enlisted two years ago, his parents applied for a program known as the Military in Place Parole program administered by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, an agency under the Department of Homeland Security. Under PIP guidelines, noncitizen parents of enlistees already inside the U.S. are eligible to apply for permission to remain in the country in one-year increments. Applications are reviewed on a case-by-case basis, according to the USCIS website.

Martinez said his parents’ applications have not been ruled on since they were filed. I sent an email message to the USCIS seeking a status update for Ruiz’s request but was denied any information.

“Generally speaking, and as a matter of practice, USCIS does not comment on individual immigration cases,” USCIS public affairs officials wrote in an email.

Because of Martinez’s National Guard service, his father’s lack of a violent criminal history and pending removal proceedings against him, the USCIS should fast track Ruiz’s case. Otherwise, the KCK man could be deported from a country he has called home for a quarter-century.

In the face of that very real probability, there’s no wonder Martinez, a natural-born U.S. citizen, feels betrayed by his own country.

text:
Renee Good’s family is suing the Trump administration and several federal officials over her fatal shooting by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer during an operation in Minneapolis in January, her family announced on Thursday.

In two civil lawsuits filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, Good’s family asserts a wrongful death claim against the United States and accuses federal officials and immigration enforcement agents of violating her civil rights, respectively.

Benjamin Berkman, one of the attorneys, said at a news conference on Thursday morning that the lawsuits “address two distinct but related evils.” One, which names the United States as a defendant, is about the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement operation in Minnesota, he said.

The second lawsuit, Berkman said, was about the “excessive force” deployed by ICE agents, including Jonathan Ross, who killed Good. White House aide Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her former aide Corey Lewandowski, former Border Patrol commander Greg Bovino, and Ross are named as defendants in the second complaint.

The lawsuits come almost nine months after Good, a 37-year-old mother, was shot and killed in her car as she attempted to drive away from ICE officers, bystander video showed. The Trump administration, however, characterized her as the aggressor and said Ross shot her — repeatedly — in self-defense.

The Department of Homeland Security said it launched an investigation into the shooting, but no details or updates have been released, and the status of that investigation is unclear. DHS did not immediately respond to MS NOW’s questions about the probe.

The Justice Department declined to launch a separate probe at the time, and instead tried to investigate Good for possible criminal liability.

More articles

In her first public remarks since January, Becca Good, Renee’s partner, spoke emotionally about her family’s loss.

“Every morning, she’s my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama. How I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” she told reporters Thursday, her voice breaking.

“What happened to us should never happen to any family,” she added. “True accountability and change is the only way to make sure that no other family has to go through what we have.”

Good’s killing led to an outpouring of anger across Minneapolis, which had already been bristling against the presence and conduct of thousands of federal officers involved in the operation. Less than three weeks after Good was killed, ICE agents fatally shot another Minneapolis-area resident, Alex Pretti.

text:
The family of an American woman shot and killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent has filed two civil lawsuits related to her death, according to court records filed Thursday in Minnesota federal court.

Renee Good was killed January 7 by ICE agent Jonathan Ross in Minneapolis during the height of the Department of Homeland Security’s Operation Metro Surge, prompting significant protest in the city and sparking national outrage.

“The hole in my family and myself, created by my sister’s passing, is hauntingly apparent,” Good’s brother and plaintiff, Brent Ganger, said at a Thursday news conference announcing the lawsuits.

“Since Renee’s death, no meaningful change has occurred. The deaths of innocent Americans by taxpayer-funded government agents should not be a partisan issue, and it should alarm every American.”

One lawsuit names the United States of America as the sole defendant under the Federal Tort Claims Act, a federal law that allows people to sue the US government for personal injury, property damage or death, caused by alleged negligence of federal employees acting within their job duties.

The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory damages for Good’s partner, who witnessed the shooting, and “for the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family,” the family’s attorneys said in a statement.

In January, attorneys sent letters to the federal agencies connected with Good’s death, notifying them of their intention to pursue legal action. Under FTCA guidelines, they waited six months for a response, which could be a denial, agreement to payment, or simply a non-response, attorney Sarah Raisch said.

“We are here today because we have not heard from the government, either that they will accept the claim, or not,” attorney Antonio Romanucci said.

A tort lawsuit against the federal government, from guilt or innocence to the amount of a potential award, is typically decided by a federal judge.

In their second lawsuit, Good’s family alleges, among other things, Operation Metro Surge was “a carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors” to interfere with the civil rights of Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin, and to silence “the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign.”

The suit names Ross, ten John Doe federal agents, and several current and former Trump administration officials as defendants, including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, White House border czar Tom Homan, former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem, and Greg Bovino, the former Border Patrol official who led the administration’s immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis.

CNN has reached out to the White House, DHS, Bovino and phone numbers listed under Noem’s name for comment.

The lawsuit alleges the shots fired by Ross were “the predictable and intended product of the operation,” according to the family’s attorneys.

The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages.

‘Like trying to live without the sun’

Good’s partner and plaintiff, Becca Good, spoke publicly for the first time since the deadly shooting took place. During the Thursday news conference, she called Good “the center” of her universe and spoke about taking their 6-year-old son to first grade without her.

“Living without her is like trying to live without the sun. And you don’t know how much light something gives you until it’s gone, and then you feel that absence every single second,” she said, becoming emotional.

Renee Good loved her three children, her partner said, and enjoyed reading them books, and talking about music and comics with them.

“Every morning, she is my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama, and how I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” she said. “But I also think a lot about what she would have wanted after all of this.”

Becca Good said the family is pursuing legal action because “Renee’s love and legacy demand a better world for her children, for this community, and for this country.”

“What happened to us should never happen to any family,” Good said. “Accountability and change — true accountability — is the only way to make sure that no other family has to go through what we have.”

“I don’t hate the people who took Renee from us, but what I want them to understand is - every single day, they get to look at their children, and their wives, and their sisters, and know what they took from our family,” Good said. “They took a mother away from her children. They know that, and they will carry it forever.”

How the deadly shooting unfolded in Minneapolis

Good, a mother of three, had just finished dropping her 6-year-old son off at school when she encountered ICE agents.

The moments leading up to the shooting were captured by bystanders as well as Ross, a 10-year ICE veteran, whose cellphone video starts with him in front of Good’s burgundy SUV. The vehicle was stopped for a few minutes perpendicular to a snowy residential Minneapolis street, obstructing the flow of traffic.

Ross did not say anything as he walked from the front of the car toward the driver’s side.

Good then addressed Ross, the video shows.

“That’s fine, dude. I’m not mad at you,” she says. Ross didn’t respond.

Becca Good was standing outside the car and said “show your face” to Ross, whose masked reflection is seen on the vehicle’s windows as he continues walking around it. Becca Good holds her cellphone up, seemingly recording Ross, and tells him, “You wanna come at us? You wanna come at us? I say go get yourself some lunch, big boy.”

She then tries to get back into the car, but the door is locked.

Another officer then tells Renee Good to “get out of the f**king car.”

Renee Good is then seen reversing the car and glancing forward as she turns the steering wheel to the right. The car moves forward, Ross cries out, “whoa,” and three gunshots are heard. Good was shot shortly after 9:30 a.m., according to a news release from the city government.

The video filmed by Ross captured audio of gunshots but doesn’t show the actual moment of the shooting, though other video from bystanders shows Ross was standing out of the vehicle’s path when he opened fire. He fired first into her windshield and then at close range through the open driver’s side window, videos show.

The end of Ross’s video shows the SUV as it barrels forward. Someone can be heard saying, “f**king b*tch.”

DHS later said Good “weaponized her vehicle” to run over an officer near an ICE vehicle.

The search for accountability for the shooting remains ongoing. In March, the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office and two state agencies sued the Trump administration for access to evidence in Good’s shooting death as well as the death of Alex Pretti, who was killed by DHS agents in January.

In July, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced the Department of Justice had provided a trove of materials related to both shootings to state investigators. No charges have been filed in either case.

This story has been updated with additional information.

Here's one tool the Trump administration is using to pressure undocumented immigrants to leave the country themselves, civil fines of up to $1.8 million per person. From member station WUNC, here's Aaron Sanchez-Guerra.

TITO SABILLON: (Speaking Spanish).

SANCHEZ-GUERRA: With paint-stained hands and jeans, this is how Sabillon has made his American dream happen, ever since he migrated from Honduras more than a decade ago. But this dream is in jeopardy. This summer, Sabillon got a letter saying he owes the Department of Homeland Security more than $1 million. Sabillon is undocumented. SABILLON: I have a family. That's the only that really matters that I have over here, you know?

SANCHEZ-GUERRA: Paying the fine is out of the question, and so is leaving his U.S. citizen wife, his stepson, his business and the southern state he now calls home.

SABILLON: I don't have a reason to get back in Honduras anyway. In my country, everything can be dangerous some places where I live, you know? And I think, like, you can do well in this country if you can have a way to do good, you know?

SANCHEZ-GUERRA: Sabillon says he had no clue about a removal order, and the notice of the fines was the first time he heard about this. Lawyers have told him his best option is to try to gain legal status through his spouse. DHS says in a statement that by mid-July, it had issued more than 100,000 civil fines, totaling more than $84 billion. DHS says those fines include up to $1,000 for each day that a person hasn't self-deported since receiving a removal order. Sabillon's family, like his father-in-law, Ricky Robinson, has come to his defense.

RICKY ROBINSON: Where's he going to get $1 million, out of his back pocket? That's a scare tactic.

SANCHEZ-GUERRA: Robinson voted for Trump in the 2024 election. He says he regrets his decision now.

ROBINSON: He said that he was going to get the criminal aliens. If you're - just 'cause you came across the border, and you've done nothing but start your business, start a family and haven't committed any crimes, no, he never said anything about going after people like that.

SANCHEZ-GUERRA: Immigration policy swings with each administration. But Congress set up the conditions of a flawed system, says Aaron Reichlin-Melnick of the American Immigration Council.

AARON REICHLIN-MELNICK: The last time Congress made any changes to our immigration enforcement system was 1996.

SANCHEZ-GUERRA: That law blocks people from returning to the U.S. for up to 10 years if they had unlawful presence. But it also kept a lot of migrants from leaving the U.S. when, historically, they would move back and forth, says Reichlin-Melnick.

REICHLIN-MELNICK: Twenty-five, 30 years later, we are seeing the problems of a system where no one can fix their papers until Congress actually gets its act together and changes the law.

SANCHEZ-GUERRA: Today's government says these immigrants have willfully failed to self-deport. But many have stayed while trying to get legal status, says Hasan Shafiqullah with The Legal Aid Society of New York.

HASAN SHAFIQULLAH: If I'm on a pathway to get a green card through my U.S. citizen spouse - self-petition, green card, whatever, there's so many different ways that people get status in this country - why should I self-deport?

text:
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case focused on the Trump administration’s policy requiring millions of undocumented immigrants to remain in detention while they fight deportation.

The case, accepted on Thursday by the justices, is the latest dispute over US President Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown to reach the nation’s highest court.

list 2 of 3Venezuelan man shot by ICE officer in Texas is charged with assault

list 3 of 3US judge rules Wisconsin mosque leader Salah Sarsour can be deported

end of list

At issue is whether migrants already living in the US have a legal right to a hearing where a judge can decide whether they should be released on bond from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention while their deportation cases are pending.

In July 2025, the administration introduced new guidance directing federal immigration authorities to detain undocumented immigrants without a bond hearing for the duration of their deportation proceedings, which can last for years.

The new policy, which has divided lower courts, reverses a decades-old interpretation that allowed some immigrants in the US to be released while their cases were pending in immigration court, according to Reuters news agency.

Most US federal appeals courts have ruled that immigrants cannot be detained without a bond hearing. But the 5th and 8th US Circuit Courts of Appeals have found that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the country must remain detained while their deportation cases proceed.

Trump administration attorneys told the Associated Press the split is “disrupting the orderly administration of immigration law”.

“The result is an unworkable patchwork of inconsistent immigration enforcement, where aliens present without admission are subject to mandatory detention in some circuits but are entitled to bond hearings and often released in others,” the lawyers wrote.

Millions could be affected

The Supreme Court case stems from a 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruling involving Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian national who entered the US around 2004 or 2005.

Immigration officers arrested him in September 2025 while he was driving to work in the US state of Massachusetts. He was initially denied a bond hearing under the administration’s policy but was later released on bond, according to court documents cited by Reuters.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), which is representing the plaintiffs, told the Associated Press the Trump administration is trying to deny bond hearings for immigrants apprehended within the US rather than limiting the restriction to noncitizens stopped at the border.

“Millions of noncitizens could be affected by the government’s new interpretation,” ACLU attorneys wrote.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments on Monday, when its new term starts.

The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in the state of Minnesota, has sued the government over her killing during a sweeping immigrant deportation blitz in January.

The two lawsuits – filed on Thursday by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother, Brent Ganger – say officials from US President Donald Trump’s administration were reckless and violated the civil rights of Good and others in Minneapolis. The lawsuits are demanding a jury trial and financial damages.

The lawsuits are the first major civil actions taken against the Trump administration over its unprecedented deportation crackdowns in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.

The first lawsuit seeks damages for Good’s wrongful death under Minnesota law, citing claims of assault, battery, false imprisonment, negligence and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

The second lawsuit alleges a civil rights conspiracy among numerous defendants including the immigration officer and shooter Jonathon Ross, who was named alongside high-ranking Trump administration officials, including White House Deputy Policy Chief Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino and Trump’s longtime campaign adviser, Corey Lewandowski.

Good, a mother of three, was shot and killed in her car by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent in south Minneapolis when she and her wife joined one of the city’s daily demonstrations against masked and armed federal agents deployed to the city to arrest migrants for deportation.

Widespread cellphone footage taken by eyewitnesses captured the moment in which Good was killed, after agent Ross fired into the windshield, shooting her in the head, arm and torso.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”.

In a statement posted on Truth Social at the time, Trump defended the deadly ICE shooting, saying that the reason those “incidents” were happening was that “the Radical Left is threatening, assaulting, and targeting our Law Enforcement Officers and ICE Agents on a daily basis”.

Days after the shooting, officials from the US Department of Justice, including then-Deputy Attorney Todd Blanche, blocked federal prosecutors from pursuing a criminal civil rights case against the agents involved in her killing, which prompted at least half a dozen of those prosecutors to resign in protest.

Minnesota sued the Trump administration in March to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes, but investigations stalled after the Justice Department halted its routine cooperation and evidence-sharing with the Minneapolis Police Department.

None of the agents involved in Good’s killing has faced any charges.

text:
WASHTENAW COUNTY, Mich. — A Trinity Health Ann Arbor nurse is facing a federal criminal charge after prosecutors say she helped an immigration detainee escape from the hospital while he was in U.S. Border Patrol custody.

Chloe Renae Freeman has been charged with one count of instigating or assisting escape, a misdemeanor that carries up to one year in prison. She has pleaded not guilty. Her next court date is Oct. 20.

Freeman made her initial court appearance in Detroit on Tuesday and was released on a $10,000 unsecured bond.

You can watch Ruta Ulcinaite's full report below:

Ann Arbor nurse charged with helping ICE detainee escape from Trinity Health hospital

According to a federal criminal complaint filed Aug. 28 in the Eastern District of Michigan, U.S. Border Patrol agents conducted a targeted immigration enforcement operation on May 28 in Ann Arbor. Agents approached the man, identified in court documents only by the initials OBP, near the intersection of Washtenaw Avenue and Pittsfield Boulevard. OBP is described as a native and citizen of Mexico who had previously been removed from the United States on or about Dec. 12, 2022, from Arizona.

When agents approached OBP, they claim he fled, tripped over a curb and hit his face on the pavement. After agents took him into custody, they observed bleeding from his head and contacted Emergency Medical Services. EMS transported OBP to Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital for further evaluation.

The complaint states that after OBP completed a CT scan, Freeman came to the CT scan room and told the operator to hold OBP and not return him to his room. Badge swipe data from the hospital showed Freeman accessed the second-floor CT Room on May 28. Security video footage then showed OBP exiting the hospital through the ambulance bay door.

The complaint states that during a hospital interview on June 18, Freeman admitted to letting OBP leave. She said she knew he was an ICE custody patient but claimed she did not believe he was in custody at the time because ICE agents were not physically with him in the CT room. The complaint states Freeman removed OBP's IV and escorted him out through the ambulance bay doors before he was properly discharged and before his hospital care was complete.

The complaint states Freeman told investigators she did not agree with ICE separating people from their families and that she "knew she was going to set him free." Law enforcement has been unable to locate OBP since his escape from the hospital.

Immigration attorney at Atiya Law, Shahad Atiya, who is also a professor at UM Dearborn, said the charge against Freeman is unusual.

"It's alleging a violation of federal law, a misdemeanor violation that could carry up to one year in prison," Atiya said. "We haven't seen it yet in the space where we deal with immigration offenses. I think this is going to be probably a new set of charges that are targeting people who are looking to assist immigrants in one way or another," Atiya said.

Diego Bonesatti, legal services program manager with Michigan United, said his organization has been tracking ICE arrests across Michigan and that the incident in Washtenaw County does not surprise him.

"Given the lack of training of new ICE recruits and the massive amount of spending and hiring, it does not surprise me that people are getting hurt," Bonesatti said.

Laura Sanders, co-founder of the Movement for Immigrant Rights Action or MIRA, says the defendant has her organization, and others, in her corner.

"We as advocates and activists in this area have respect for her attempt to protect this immigrant man," Sanders said.

Trinity Health Ann Arbor released a statement regarding the incident:

"The individual referenced is no longer employed by Trinity Health Ann Arbor. Because this is an active legal matter, we are unable to comment on the specific allegations or ongoing court proceedings."

The criminal complaint was filed by FBI Special Agent Michael Wagner and signed by U.S. Magistrate Judge Kimberly Altman. The case was initially sealed before being unsealed ahead of Freeman's court appearance.

Renee Good was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.

Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver's seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.

Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, "get out of the car."

Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: "Drive, baby, drive!"

One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver's side, fires two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in "an act of domestic terrorism."

One lawsuit alleges wrongful death

The lawsuit, which seeks a bench trial, also alleges "intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress" on Becca Good.

Becca and Renee Good, the mother of three children, were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.

Another lawsuit alleges conspiracy to conceal evidence

The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial. It says the federal government moved to hide the evidence of what actually happened on Jan. 7.

text:
A preliminary injunction is a temporary court order issued before a case is finally decided that requires a party to take or stop an action while the litigation continues. Federal courts generally consider likelihood of success, irreparable harm, the balance of equities, and the public interest before granting one.

A preliminary injunction is a form of temporary judicial relief designed to protect the parties or preserve meaningful relief while a lawsuit is pending.

Unlike a final judgment, a preliminary injunction is issued before the court has fully resolved the merits of the case.

In federal civil litigation, preliminary injunctions are governed by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65. State courts have their own procedural rules and standards.

What Must Someone Show to Obtain a Preliminary Injunction?

The Supreme Court set out the modern federal framework in Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council.

A party seeking a preliminary injunction generally must establish a likelihood of success on the merits, a likelihood of irreparable harm without preliminary relief, that the balance of equities favors the requested order, and that an injunction is in the public interest.

The Supreme Court has emphasized that a preliminary injunction is an extraordinary remedy, not something a party receives automatically just because a lawsuit has been filed.

What Is Irreparable Harm?

Irreparable harm generally means an injury that cannot be adequately corrected through ordinary legal relief after the case is finished.

In Winter, the Supreme Court rejected a standard based merely on the possibility of irreparable injury. The party seeking relief ordinarily must establish that the injury is likely in the absence of an injunction.

Preliminary Injunctions and Death Penalty Litigation

Preliminary injunctions sometimes play a central role in method-of-execution litigation.

A prisoner facing an execution date can seek an injunction preventing officials from using a disputed procedure while the constitutional challenge is litigated. Because the execution would make later judicial relief impossible, questions of irreparable harm are particularly significant.

The prisoner must still satisfy the standards governing extraordinary equitable relief, including a sufficient showing on the underlying constitutional claim.

Preliminary Injunction Versus Final Injunction

A preliminary injunction operates while litigation remains pending.

A permanent injunction is entered after the court resolves the legal dispute and determines that permanent equitable relief is appropriate.

Granting preliminary relief does not mean the party seeking the injunction will ultimately win the case.

irreparable harm

stay of execution

text:
For 25-year-old Catherine Rax, another day inside a cell at the Flagler County Jail is another day spent wondering what comes next.

“It’s not living — it’s surviving,” she told the Tallahassee Democrat.

You may not recognize her name. You may not even remember her face at the local eatery. But you have seen her before — in headlines, across social media, in that traumatic moment captured on surveillance video. A moment that would change her life and the lives of those around her forever.

On Friday, Sept. 25, a traffic stop that escalated into an immigration-enforcement operation at beloved local food establishment Chile & Chili's Taqueria became the center of a broader conversation about immigration enforcement in Tallahassee.

Days later, nearly 100 local community members rallied around the Mexican eatery at its now permanently closed West Tennessee Street location with the help of the Tallahassee Community Area Response Equipo (TCARE), which is the Leon County hub for the Florida Immigrant Coalition as well as the Tallahassee Immigrant Rights Alliance.

Wednesday night made it evident that the space that once served as a designated hangout spot to indulge in a taste of Oaxaca and catch up with friends has been stained with the events of that day.

"The people united... will never be defeated," the crowd chanted as they held signs and waved their flags. Children and elders, students and young professionals of every background gathered in front of the trucks that Wednesday night.

Among them were Rax’s friends, who held up a tablet so she could see the crowd gathered in her honor. From inside the jail, she watched the community rally around her, an attempt to lift her spirits and remind her that people cared.

While that 20-second surveillance video may make the impact feel distant, the Tallahassee Democrat came face-to-face with Rax through a tablet inside the county jail. For 10 emotional minutes, she shared her story before the call timed out.

"Honestly, I’m very sad… they’re not just my coworkers; they’re my family," Rax said, clinging to the phone for strength as she held back tears. Rax has no immediate family with her in Tallahassee.

Rax worked the stand, where coworkers had become some of the people she leaned on most.

Every dollar she earned carried more weight as her mother battles cancer, she'd often send the money she made back home to help with the family and medical expenses. Before her detention, survival meant showing up to work, helping her family and making it through another day. From inside the walls of the county jail, survival looks a lot different.

Now, Rax is separated from her family and loved ones, waiting inside the county jail, and she has no idea what awaits.

"What questions do I have? I have so many. When am I going to get out of here? How long am I going to last here? How long will I be here? When will I be able to see my family?… I didn't ask to be illegal," Rax said.

Along with Rax, two men were detained, including her partner.

One of them is now in the state-run immigration detention facility nicknamed "Deportation Depot" in Baker County. All three were originally from Guatemala.

"We were a family … always cheerful, always dancing, there was always music, working, and cooking … wholesome, good-hearted people. Remembering the innocence of such good people, what is happening hurts deep in the soul," Chile & Chili's owner Marco Tenorio said.

Hours after the rally, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sent a statement to the Tallahassee Democrat confirming the operation, stating that they did not "target the taqueria" and the three detained at the taco stand "attempted to flee" and "entered the United States illegally."

"They don't realize the mental harm they are causing, and that all of this will have consequences … But on the other hand, I feel very good about how the people are supporting us. The outpouring of support has been incredible … it gives you that feeling where you say to yourself, 'I did something right,' " Tenorio said.

Zolia Virgen Verduzco, by way of Quincy, made her way through the crowds, thanking individuals for showing their support.

For Verduzco, the rally hit close to home; just recently, her brother, who lived in the country for 45 years, was detained and deported to Mexico, she says, despite having legal counsel and documentation processes underway, and thousands she's paid in legal fees.

"It means a lot to us because sometimes it feels good to know that someone cares," she said. "I really feel, honestly, that it's time for all of us to get together, to be united."

text:
North Carolina’s first immigration detention center is set to open in the state’s northeastern corner before year’s end. Though activists have protested against the center, some residents say they don’t sense that opposition in their communities and look forward to the facility’s projected economic gains.

The GEO Group, one of the world’s largest federal prison contractors and owner of Rivers Correctional Institution in Winton, said in July that it signed a five-year contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to reopen the 1,320-bed facility this year as Winton ICE Processing Center.

The facility lies on the edge of Hertford County, about 20 miles south of the Virginia state line; it’s surrounded by trees and rural farmland. The facility closed in 2021 after President Joe Biden issued an executive order to terminate all federal contracts with private prisons.

Before it closed, Rivers had high rates of inmate grievances, positive drug tests and inmate-on-inmate sexual assault according to a 2016 federal report. However, it employed hundreds of people, and some locals The News & Observer interviewed said the pay was enough to support middle-class lifestyles.

In July, an unnamed state official told The New York Times, which first reported the center’s opening, that it could open as early as late September. But the center had yet to open as October arrived. Construction continued near the front gate and 47 job postings were on The GEO Group’s careers page.

Rainier Bradshaw, 15, who lives in Winton and Murfreesboro — Hertford County towns with a combined population of less than 4,000 — started protesting the center earlier this year, speaking at a county commissioners meeting. She was scared to express herself so publicly, she said, but seeing others coming together to oppose the center gave her hope that they could stop the soon-to-be-detention center’s progress.

At a local protest Saturday, Bradshaw said it might now be “a little too late to hope that it’s not going to open at all.”

She added, “I hope that maybe something can be done quickly after it opens to close it again, or that it won’t just be another place of pain and suffering.”

ICE facility isn’t ‘on the radar’ for many locals

On Saturday, workers at the facility stood behind the entrance gate and watched as 50 protesters marched up and down the country road leading to the Winton facility.

But many of the protesters weren’t locals. During the march, they shouted out the places from which they’d come — Wilmington; the Outer Banks; Chapel Hill; Durham; Jones County; Virginia.

Ray Bradshaw, 55, Rainier’s father, said he wouldn’t be surprised if most locals didn’t know that the center was reopening as an ICE facility. When he speaks to people in town, it never comes up in conversation, he said.

Alison Brown, 58, who lives in Winton and Richmond, said Monday that neither she nor her husband, Mark Brown, had heard about Saturday’s protest before it happened.

“For it to be 50 people … that tells me that it wasn’t on the radar for the citizens around here,” she said.

Mark Brown said: “If (protesters from out of town) don’t live in this area … a lot of them are probably not impacted.”

Organizations beyond Hertford County have propelled the movement opposing the prison’s conversion detention center. Stop Detention Centers NC, a statewide grassroots organization, collected donations to pay for a $1,100 billboard in Ahoskie condemning the center earlier this year. They have also sent postcards to residents with a message echoing the billboard.

Jessica Burroughs, an organizer at The Workers Circle, a national nonprofit promoting social justice, said that her group’s advocacy is “just getting started” and that by continuing to protest, activists will draw locals’ eyes.

“Our criticism for the facility is not criticism of the people who are taking these jobs because they need the income. They are not the enemy here,” Burroughs said. “Our focus is on these private facilities and how much money is being given to those folks at the top running these institutions.”

Caroline Stephenson, a Hertford County resident and the protest’s primary organizer, said that as the center’s opening nears, protesters will keep marching, at least once a month.

The GEO Group did not respond to repeated requests for comment by The News & Observer.

Some locals see center’s economic opportunities

Mark Brown, 65, said he remembers getting paid to pick tobacco as a teenager.

“My whole family worked in the field,” Brown said. “Everyone got the experience of hard work.”

But as technology and farming equipment advanced, “it cut generations of people with jobs off,” he said. That makes bringing jobs like the ones at Winton ICE Processing Center all the more important, he said.

When Rivers was open, he said, people who worked there could make enough money to buy homes and have a good quality of life, Brown said. The closure cost 350 workers their jobs.

The facility had a job fair in August. Some former workers at Rivers have received communication from The GEO Group inviting them to return.

However, 10 of the 43 jobs Winston-based jobs listed on The GEO Group’s website that are based in Winton pay less than $42,000 a year, $3,000 shy of Hertford County’s median income, although salaries for detention center-related medical jobs, such as dentists, physicians and nurses, reach six figures.

Donnie Taylor, 75, a retired lawyer who lives in Bertie County, just 2 miles from the Hertford County border, said he doesn’t hear any complaints about the center, calling them “rumors.” With limited job opportunities in the area, he believes that the jobs it will bring should overshadow concerns.

“Anything coming to the area is good,” he said. “The people in the community where I live … my contacts and what I deal with … there isn’t just outrage for ICE.”

Taylor said he believes that “there’s more to worry about down here” than the detention center. He said more focus should be committed to addressing violent crime, gangs and drugs and that he wouldn’t mind having more law enforcement present in the area, even if it’s immigration authorities.

Numbers show crime rising in Hertford County. In 2023, the latest year with available data, the county, population 19,000, had 60 incidents of violent crime, a 30% increase from a year earlier, a 2025 report by the state’s Department of Public Safety shows. During the same period, Bertie County had 57 violent crimes, up 16% from a year earlier. The department broadly defines violent crimes as homicide, aggravated assault and rape.

Crime statistics notwithstanding, Ahoskie native Bobby Ray Riddick was warier of the detention center than Taylor. He said he’d cut ties with anyone who chooses to work there.

“What if it was your child that was being locked up?” said Riddick, who has protested against the center. “So you feel that the money, it outweighs someone that’s being incarcerated (wrongfully)?”

‘Most important contributor’ to the NC anti-detention center movement

Riddick, 62, started frequently driving by the center, livestreaming to his 10,000 followers on Facebook earlier this year. He said he’s not afraid of any local blowback.

“When you start talking about what’s going on in a community and people are scared to speak out because it’s being run by people who are from here that’s holding positions and they use their authority to intimidate people,” Riddick said. “I’m retired. I don’t have anything to lose. … So, I can freely speak up to how I feel without threat.”

Liz Dreesen, an organizer with Stop Detention Centers NC, said Riddick has boosted her group’s advocacy.

“Everybody tunes in to Bobby Ray because Bobby Ray does a lot of talking about what’s going on in the … Hertford County world,” Dreesen said. “Having Bobby Ray talk us up is probably the most important contributor to people knowing about what we’re doing.”

There’s more to the region than an ICE center, locals say

Booker Daniel, 67, who opposes the ICE facility, grew up near Stephenson, one of the movement’s primary organizers. Their homes in Murfreesboro were near a deep gully filled with sprawling trees and kudzu. They called themselves “gully girls.”

Daniel, a retired social worker, said she promised herself years ago to not work at Rivers.

“I’m glad I made that choice,” she said. “Not all money is good money.”

Daniel supports Stephenson in her movement against the detention center, though she understands why people want jobs there.

“Everything is so expensive right now,” she said.

Although the town is making headlines for the detention center, Daniel said that she wants “people to know that there’s more out here than the ICE facility.”

Once a month, she leads “Storytelling for Grown Folk,” a session at which she teaches about the town’s history to adults at the library.

Daniel said she enjoys talking about historic Murfreesboro, especially Murfrees Landing, a now defunct port and mill site that was once Murfreesboro’s claim to fame. She loves telling the story of Hannah Crafts, an enslaved woman famous for writing a novel during her enslavement, whose historic home is just a few minutes’ drive from where the Daniels’ family home had been.

That history is what she wants the region to be known for.
